sentences.text: The name Dicraeosaurus refers to the distinctive neural spines located on the back of the animal's neck.
Unlike most diplodocoids, Dicraeosaurus possessed a comparatively large head and a relatively short, wide neck.
There is a crest or comb-like structure on the back of the head.
Dicraeosaurus measured between 13 and 20 meters in length, up to 6 meters in height, and weighed 15 tons.
Dicraeosaurus could reach up to 20 meters in length, of which 2.4 meters belonged to the neck.
Dicraeosaurus had up to 12 cervical vertebrae containing numerous air spaces, especially developed at the back of the neck.
Numerous attempts to estimate its mass yielded varied results, placing the mass of D. hansemanni between 10 and 40 tons.
The tail of Dicraeosaurus, which acted like a whip, could be used for defense or to make loud sounds.
Calculations indicate that Dicraeosaurus contained 974 liters of air, with a 48-kilogram heart pumping 641 liters of blood at a rate of 23 beats per minute.
The first fossils of Dicraeosaurus were described by paleontologist Werner Janensch in 1914.
Fossils of Dicraeosaurus were found in the Tendaguru Formation in Tanzania and possibly in Kazdi, Zimbabwe.
Researchers suggest the tall neural spines likely provided attachment points for muscles.
These spines served as insertion points for powerful neck muscles.
Researchers Martin and colleagues suggest that a cervical ligament played a decisive role in maintaining the neck position.
It is suggested that Dicraeosaurus maintained an upright neck and bent head while walking on extended legs.
Some experts believe the neck of Dicraeosaurus could have been inclined, though a horizontal position is not excluded.
The neck of Dicraeosaurus contained 12 unusually short vertebrae, suggesting it was a low-level browser feeding on vegetation no more than 3 meters off the ground.
The peg-shaped teeth of Dicraeosaurus were ideal for feeding on plants.
Dicraeosaurus could eat hard foods like cycads thanks to its wide teeth.

While some authors suggest the skull structure indicates biting movements adapted for cutting food, others interpret it as front-to-back movements typical of earlier sauropods adapted for pulling food.
Dicraeosaurus was a herbivore that did not compete with other dinosaurs for food.
In 2008, Lehman and Woodward estimated that a mature adult Dicraeosaurus lived for 11 to 22 years and grew at an average rate of 227 to 455 kg per year.
Dicraeosaurus grew rapidly and without interruption to its maximum size, reaching sexual maturity at 80% of that maximum size.
The long neck of sauropods like Dicraeosaurus may have evolved as a result of sexual selection.
The genus Dicraeosaurus has been synonymized with Issasaurus, Mtotosaurus, Nyororosaurus, and Selimanosaurus.
Since 1991, Dicraeosaurus has been classified in the family Dicraeosauridae, part of the superfamily Diplodocoidea.
The family Dicraeosauridae is believed to be more evolutionarily advanced than the family Diplodocidae.
A 2005 study by Rauhut confirmed that Dicraeosaurus is monophyletic and more closely related to Brachytrachelopan than to Amargasaurus.
Dicraeosaurus was a mid-sized herbivore found in the Tendaguru Formation of Tanzania, which dates to the Late Jurassic.
Dicraeosaurus lived during the late Jurassic period, approximately 156 to 145 million years ago, between the Oxfordian and Tithonian stages, in what is now Africa.
Dicraeosaurus hansemanni lived between the Oxfordian and Kimeridgian stages, while D. sattleri lived during the Tithonian stage.
Dicraeosaurus lived from the Oxfordian to the Tithonian stages, approximately 161.5 to 143.1 million years ago.
The hypothesis that Dicraeosaurus stopped growing earlier than its relatives is supported by the poor pneumatization of its bones.
